sources.title: Italy's $4.7 billion cheese economy is feeling the heat as climate change threatens its cheese banks
Italy's Parmesan Industry Under Pressure as Extreme Heat Cuts Milk Production
Europe's 40C Heatwave Threatens Parmesan Cheese Production
Italy's cheese banks feel the heat (video, Reuters)

chunks.text: A long [[heatwave]] in northern Italy is {{cutting into}} the country's most famous cheese. When the air goes above 40 degrees Celsius, which is 104 Fahrenheit, [[dairy cows]] eat less and give [[up to]] ten [[percent]] less milk. Parmigiano Reggiano is made from that milk. The [[producers]] who {{stand behind}} the name sell about four [[billion]] euros of cheese a year, and a farmer cannot {{make up}} the milk that a hot summer {{takes away}}.

verbs.correct: To reduce the amount of something
verbs.wrong: To move milk from farm to dairy
verbs.why: Heavy rain can cut into a farmer's wheat harvest for the whole season, and rising prices are cutting into many family budgets this year. This long heatwave is cutting into how much milk Italy's dairy cows can produce.

verbs.wrong: To wait for cheese to be ready
verbs.why: A good store stands behind every item it sells, and a manager should stand behind a decision once it is made. The producers who stand behind the Parmigiano Reggiano name protect a reputation built over many years.

verbs.correct: To replace something that was lost
verbs.wrong: To decide the price of a product
verbs.why: A student might make up a missed class the following week, and a team sometimes tries to make up points lost in the first half. A farmer cannot make up the milk that a long, hot summer has already cost the herd.

verbs.correct: To remove something a person had
verbs.wrong: To store cheese for a longer time
verbs.why: An injury can take away a player's chance in the finals, and a bad flu can take away your energy for a week. A hot summer literally takes away milk that dairy farmers count on for their income.

chunks.text: The cheese also [[takes a long time]] to make. A [[wheel]] must [[sit]] for [[at least]] twelve months, and most are kept for two or three years. About four million wheels a year come from around 300 [[dairies]]. While a wheel waits in [[storage]], money has already {{gone out}} for [[feed]], work and power. No money {{comes in}} for years, so the costs {{pile up}}.

verbs.correct: To be spent and leave the farm
verbs.wrong: To be sold in another country
verbs.why: Rent money goes out on the first of every month no matter what, and cash goes out fast whenever the car needs repairs. Money for feed, labor, and power all goes out long before a wheel of cheese is ready to sell.

verbs.correct: To arrive as money that is earned
verbs.wrong: To join a group of producers
verbs.why: Extra cash comes in every summer from tourists renting rooms near the coast, and steady rent money comes in on the first of each month. No money comes in from a wheel of Parmesan for years while it slowly ages in storage.

verbs.correct: To grow into a large amount
verbs.wrong: To be counted at the end of a year
verbs.why: Unpaid bills pile up fast once payments are missed, and emails pile up in an inbox during a long vacation. With no income for years while a wheel ages, a farmer's costs pile up quickly.

chunks.text: Italian banks {{thought up}} an answer to this [[a long time ago]]. One bank has accepted cheese as [[security]] for a loan since 1953. The farmer gives the bank his wheels, the bank {{puts away}} the cheese in a [[vault]], and the farmer {{takes out}} a [[loan]] [[worth]] 60 to 80 percent of what it is worth. One vault holds more than 500,000 wheels.

verbs.correct: To invent a clever answer to a problem
verbs.wrong: To copy an idea from another country
verbs.why: A team can think up a smart fix for a tricky parking problem, and kids often think up new games out of pure boredom. Italian banks thought up a clever system decades ago: farmers could borrow against wheels of aging cheese.

verbs.correct: To store something in a safe place
verbs.wrong: To sell cheese before it is ready
verbs.why: A careful saver puts away a little money every single month, and a librarian puts away returned books at the end of each day. The bank puts away each farmer's wheels of cheese inside a locked, cool vault.

verbs.correct: To arrange a loan from a bank
verbs.wrong: To repay money that is owed
verbs.why: A young couple often takes out a loan for their first home, and a farmer might take out a small loan before spring planting. In this system, a farmer takes out a loan worth 60 to 80 percent of what the cheese is worth.

chunks.text: So the extreme heat is now affecting the banks that lend money against cheese. Less milk means fewer wheels, and fewer wheels mean the banks are holding less. Keeping those vaults cool costs about 30 percent more [[electricity]] in the hottest weeks, and the Po River has {{dried up}} to under a third of its normal [[level]]. Farmers can still {{fall back on}} the loans and {{get by}}, but there is less money left [[at the end of the year]].

verbs.correct: To lose most of its water
verbs.wrong: To be measured twice each summer
verbs.why: A backyard well can dry up completely during a long drought, and a small pond often dries up fast in extreme summer heat. The Po River has dried up to under a third of its normal level this year.

verbs.correct: To use a support when all else fails
verbs.wrong: To pay a loan later than agreed
verbs.why: A speaker might fall back on old notes if memory fails, and a family can fall back on savings when work is slow. Farmers can still fall back on these cheese loans when a bad, hot summer cuts their income.

verbs.correct: To have just enough money to live
verbs.wrong: To sell a farm and leave the business
verbs.why: A young family often gets by on a tight monthly budget, and a student can get by on a small part time salary. Farmers can still get by on these cheese loans, even though less money is left at the end of the year.

mainIdea.s: A long heatwave in northern Italy is cutting into milk supplies and squeezing Parmesan cheese output. The heat is now raising costs for banks that store cheese wheels as loan security.
mainIdea.why: The article says cows give up to 10 percent less milk in extreme heat, and cooling the bank vaults costs about 30 percent more electricity.

mainIdea.s: The heatwave has pushed Italian banks to stop lending against cheese wheels because vaults now cost too much to cool. Farmers can no longer fall back on these loans during a dry summer.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the article says farmers can still fall back on the loans and get by. The banks now pay more to keep their vaults cool in the heat.

mainIdea.s: Olive oil producers in southern Italy say a long drought this summer has cut their harvest by nearly half. Growers now worry that prices for olive oil will rise sharply before fall.
mainIdea.why: This story is about an olive oil drought in southern Italy, not about the Parmesan cheese banks in the north.

lines.text: Here's a story that connects a heatwave, cheese, and banks. Italy's Parmesan is in trouble.

Start with the cows. When the air goes above 40 degrees, they eat less and give up to ten percent less milk. Parmigiano Reggiano is made from that milk, and a farmer can't {{make up}} what a hot summer {{takes away}}.

At least twelve months per wheel, usually two or three years. While a wheel waits in storage, money has already {{gone out}} for feed, work, and power. Nothing {{comes in}} for years, so the costs {{pile up}}.
So where do banks enter the story?

[[This is my favorite part]]. Since 1953, one Italian bank has accepted cheese as security for loans. The farmer gives his wheels to the bank, the bank {{puts away}} the cheese in a vault, and the farmer {{takes out}} a loan worth 60 to 80 percent of its value.
One vault holds more than 500,000 wheels. Whoever {{thought up}} that system [[deserves a statue]].
So how does the heat reach the banks?

Less milk means fewer wheels, and fewer wheels mean the banks hold less security. Cooling the vaults costs 30 percent more electricity, and the Po River has {{dried up}} to under a third of its normal level.
They can {{fall back on}} the loans and {{get by}}, but there's less money left at the end of the year. The heat is {{cutting into}} a four-billion-euro business.
The producers who {{stand behind}} the name won't lower standards. That's the whole point of Parmigiano.
A cheese so trusted a bank will hold it. [[Only in Italy]].
